source.title: Late Stopping: Avoiding Confidently Learning from Mislabeled Examples
source.authors: Su-Qin Yuan; Lei Feng; Tong-Liang Liu

record.file_problem: none; the supplied text contains the full paper, including results, tables, and figure descriptions.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures when clean and mislabeled training examples are first classified as their given labels for consecutive epochs. This bears on the learning-order claim, but it does not reproduce the original random-label fitting experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses prior findings that DNNs fit random labels and cites Arpit et al. on learning patterns before overfitting. Those cited findings are not this study’s results. Its own Figure 1(b) description reports an ordering result relevant to V6. The tables on label-selection precision report the performance of FkL as a selection criterion; they do not directly report how many epochs clean and mislabeled examples take to be learned.
record.test_reason: Figure 1(b) reports the relative learning order of clean and mislabeled training examples using first-time sustained agreement with their given labels. This directly bears on V6, beyond using memorization as motivation for a sample-selection method.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate but incomplete. The authors propose Late Stopping, using first-time sustained agreement with given labels to remove likely mislabeled examples while retaining clean hard examples, and report improved noisy-label classification performance. They acknowledge that some mislabeled examples are learned relatively early and some rare clean examples are removed.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses iterative sample selection based on first-time k-epoch learning in noisy-label datasets; it does not reproduce the original random-label fitting procedure.
record.peer_reviewed: IEEE International Conference on Computer Vision
record.problems: The ordering result relevant to V6 is described qualitatively; the supplied text does not provide numerical values for Figure 1(b).
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 reports label-selection precision by dataset, noise type, criterion, and rank range. Those measurements compare selection criteria and do not directly report the timing of clean versus mislabeled examples, so they are not included as V6 rows. Other results concern label-selection performance, classifier accuracy, training time, or the proposed method’s sensitivity, rather than the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: Complete random labeling, near-zero training error, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Training time for true versus random labels and convergence time as corruption increases. Table 8 compares different mitigation methods instead.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit and steadily worsening test error across a corruption sweep from none to all.
Effects of adding or removing explicit regularization on random-label fitting and true-label generalization.
Direct measurement of shared-pattern acquisition and a comparison of entirely true-labeled versus entirely random-labeled datasets.

missing.what: Learning-order exceptions among falsely retained mislabeled examples: correcting their labels increases average FkL rank from 22,340.66 to 28,452.08 (+27.36%). The authors associate these examples with patterns resembling dominant subclasses of the incorrect class. Record the selected-subset condition and the comparison of wrong versus corrected labels.

record.verdict_notes: The evidence supports a predominant learning order, not a strict separation of every clean and noisy example. Selection precision and mitigation accuracy do not independently establish the other claim versions.

versions.untested_parts: Random labeling, training and test error, and whether fitting requires changes to architecture or hyperparameters.
Relative training time for true versus random labels and convergence as corruption rises.
A sweep from zero to complete random corruption, perfect training fit across that sweep, and steadily changing test error.
Whether weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation affect fitting random labels or generalization on true labels.

The paper measures when examples are classified to their given labels, not when shared real-data patterns are learned; it does not compare completely random labels with true labels or establish that labels are learned differently over the full training process.

rows.operation_detail: Describes the order in which clean and mislabeled examples first meet the FkL criterion during training.
rows.measure: Order of first-time k-epoch learning for clean versus mislabeled examples
rows.value: The text states that most mislabeled examples are classified into their given labels for consecutive k epochs only in later training stages.
rows.note: The paper gives this qualitative result in its description of a normalized histogram; it does not report numerical values for the histogram in the supplied text.
rows.check: The qualitative learning-order result is accurately recorded. ResNet-18 is inferred from the general CIFAR-10 experimental setup rather than specified in the Figure 1 description; the figure's k value and numerical histogram values are unavailable.
